Congress returns November 9 with no clear plan to fill the gap. by Abigail Mihaly November 7, 2026 November 9, 2026 Share this article: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... KEY POINTS Funding for an important federal water infrastructure loan program is expected to decrease around 80 percent after a five-year supplement ended in September. This program provides key funding to states for water infrastructure projects like replacing lead service lines. But even at its peak, federal funding fell far short of national need. Congress must figure out how much to appropriate in its annual budget. But newly elected lawmakers will also need to weigh the future of the loan program. Communities across the country are facing a federal water infrastructure funding cliff following the expiration of a bipartisan, multibillion-dollar cash infusion that Congress approved during the Biden administration. The State Revolving Funds (SRF) — which assist projects like lead pipe replacement and sewer repairs — are expected to decrease around 80 percent from last year’s levels. Congress will need to approve next year’s budget for the loan program, a foundation of federal support for local water systems, when lawmakers return on November 9. Advocates are sounding alarm bells after the recent sunset of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021. A bipartisan feat, the law quadrupled the amount of money states received via the SRF. It was a major federal effort to support the gaping need to fix water infrastructure across the country. But the extra funding — around $43 billion over five years — ended in September, and Congress doesn’t have clear plans for an extension.
